children.text: Caldwell & Associates was founded in 2001 by Jonathan Caldwell, a former federal clerk who believed that high-quality legal counsel should be accessible to growing businesses and families alike — not just to Fortune 500 companies with unlimited legal budgets.
Our story

What began as a solo practice focused on business formation has grown into a full-service firm with six attorneys, a dedicated paralegal team, and deep expertise across business law, estate planning, family law, real estate, and commercial litigation. We have handled over 1,200 matters and maintained a 98% client retention rate across more than two decades.
How we work

Every engagement starts with a thorough consultation. We listen before we advise. We explain your options in plain language, give you our honest assessment of risks and likely outcomes, and let you make an informed decision about how to proceed. You will always have a direct line to your attorney — not a voicemail box.
Our commitment

We are members of the State Bar and the American Bar Association. Our attorneys maintain active professional development and hold leadership roles in the local business community. We carry full professional liability coverage and adhere to the highest standards of legal ethics.

data.title: What Every Small Business Owner Should Know Before Signing a Contract
data.excerpt: Most business disputes start with a poorly written contract. Here are the provisions every business owner should understand before putting pen to paper.

$media.alt: Attorney reviewing contract documents at desk

children.text: Every year, business owners sign contracts they do not fully understand — and some of those contracts come back to haunt them. The good news is that most problematic provisions are predictable and can be negotiated before you sign. Here are the things we review with every business client before they execute a significant agreement.
1. Dispute resolution and governing law

Many contracts require disputes to be resolved through arbitration, often in a different state. This can make it expensive to pursue a valid claim or defend yourself against one. Always check which state's law governs the contract and where disputes must be resolved — and negotiate if those terms don't work for your business.
2. Limitation of liability clauses

Contracts often cap the damages one party can recover from the other — sometimes at a fraction of the contract value. If you are relying on a vendor or contractor for something critical to your business, a liability cap could leave you without meaningful recourse if they fail to perform.
3. Automatic renewal provisions

Service agreements frequently auto-renew for one-year terms if you do not provide written notice 60 or 90 days before the end of the current term. We have seen clients trapped in expensive contracts because they missed a cancellation window by a week. Put renewal dates on your calendar the day you sign.
Have a significant contract to review? We offer flat-fee contract review for most standard business agreements. Contact us for a quote.

data.title: The 4 Estate Planning Documents Every Adult Should Have
data.excerpt: A will is just the beginning. Here are the four documents that ensure your wishes are followed and your loved ones are protected — regardless of your age or net worth.

$media.alt: Family reviewing documents together at a table

children.text: Estate planning is not just for the wealthy or the elderly. If you own property, have children, or care about who makes decisions on your behalf if you become incapacitated, you need these four documents in place. Most clients are surprised by how straightforward the process is.
1. A last will and testament

A will directs how your assets are distributed and, if you have minor children, names a guardian. Without one, the state decides both — according to a formula that may not reflect your wishes. A properly drafted will also names an executor who can act quickly to settle your estate.
2. A durable financial power of attorney

This document authorizes someone you trust to manage your financial affairs if you are unable to do so. Without it, your family may need to go to court to obtain guardianship — a process that can take months and cost thousands of dollars, all while your bills go unpaid.
3. A healthcare proxy (medical power of attorney)

This names someone to make medical decisions on your behalf if you cannot make them yourself. Without it, medical providers may be unable to share information with your family, and disputes can arise about your care.
4. An advance healthcare directive (living will)
A living will documents your wishes regarding end-of-life care. It relieves your loved ones of an agonizing decision during an already difficult time and ensures your wishes are honored.
We offer a flat-fee estate planning package that includes all four documents, a trust consultation, and a one-year review. Contact us to schedule your estate planning consultation.

data.title: LLC, S-Corp, or C-Corp? Choosing the Right Business Structure
data.excerpt: The entity type you choose affects your taxes, liability exposure, and ability to raise capital. Here is how to think through the decision.

$media.alt: Business professionals in a meeting reviewing documents

children.text: One of the first decisions every new business owner faces is how to structure their entity. The right answer depends on your tax situation, your liability exposure, whether you plan to bring in investors, and how you want the business to be governed. Here is a plain-English breakdown of the most common structures.
Sole proprietorship

The simplest structure — no formation required. But there is no liability protection: your personal assets are exposed if the business is sued or cannot pay its debts. For anything beyond the most modest side activity, a sole proprietorship is rarely the right choice.
LLC (Limited Liability Company)

The LLC is the workhorse structure for most small and mid-sized businesses. It provides liability protection, flexible governance, and pass-through taxation. An LLC can be taxed as a sole proprietorship, partnership, S-corp, or C-corp depending on your elections — which gives you flexibility as the business grows.
Thinking about forming a new entity or restructuring an existing one? Schedule a business formation consultation and we will help you choose the structure that fits your goals.

data.title: Meridian Industrial Acquisition
data.summary: Represented the buyer in a $4.2M acquisition of a regional industrial supplier — from LOI through due diligence, financing, and closing.

$media.alt: Modern corporate boardroom with city view

children.text: Our client had identified a strategic acquisition target and needed legal counsel to move quickly without sacrificing diligence. We managed the full transaction: negotiating the purchase agreement, coordinating with the lender's counsel, conducting due diligence across corporate records, contracts, and regulatory filings, and closing within 90 days of the signed LOI.
Outcome

Transaction closed on schedule with favorable indemnification terms negotiated by our team. Two post-closing issues identified in due diligence were resolved through purchase price adjustments before closing, saving our client a potential six-figure exposure.

data.title: Whitmore Family Estate Restructure
data.summary: Restructured a multi-generational family estate including revocable trust, family LLC, and charitable remainder trust to minimize estate tax exposure.

$media.alt: Estate planning documents and family heirlooms

children.text: A family with significant real property holdings and investment assets sought to restructure their estate in anticipation of generational transfer. Working closely with their CPA, we designed a plan that transferred assets to a family LLC, established a revocable living trust as the primary vehicle, and created a charitable remainder trust to provide income while reducing taxable estate value.
Result

The restructured plan reduced estimated estate tax exposure by approximately 38% while preserving family control over operating assets and establishing a charitable legacy aligned with the family's values.

data.title: Hartley Construction — Contract Dispute
data.summary: Represented a regional contractor in a $1.8M dispute over a commercial build-out contract. Resolved through mediation in under six months.

$media.alt: Attorney reviewing case files in courtroom

children.text: Our client, a general contractor, was accused of defective work and breach of contract by a commercial building owner seeking $1.8M in damages. After reviewing the project record, we identified significant evidence that the defects were attributable to design errors and owner-directed changes. We filed counterclaims for unpaid contract balance and extras.
Outcome

The matter was resolved in mediation. The owner's claims were dismissed in full and our client recovered a substantial portion of the unpaid contract balance. Total resolution time: five months from engagement to settlement.

data.question: How does the initial consultation work?

children.text: We offer a 30-minute initial consultation by phone or video, or in person at our office. During the consultation, we will listen to your matter, ask clarifying questions, give you our honest assessment, and explain how we would approach the representation. There is no obligation to retain us after the consultation.

We offer flat fees for transactional work (estate planning packages, business formation, contract review) and hourly rates for litigation and complex matters. Our hourly rates are disclosed upfront, and we provide written fee agreements before beginning any engagement. We do not bill in 6-minute increments for every email.

data.question: Which clients and courts do you serve?

children.text: We serve clients throughout the greater metro area and surrounding counties. Our attorneys are admitted in state and federal courts in this jurisdiction. We also handle matters in neighboring states through co-counsel arrangements when needed. Consultations are available in-person, by phone, or via video conference.

data.question: How long will my matter take?

children.text: Timelines vary considerably by matter type. A standard estate plan is typically completed within three to four weeks. A straightforward business acquisition takes 60 to 90 days. Contested litigation depends on court scheduling and opposing counsel, but we will give you a realistic timeline at the outset and update you whenever it changes.

For flat-fee matters, we can often structure payments in installments. For hourly matters, we require an initial retainer and bill monthly against it. We accept all major credit cards, check, and ACH transfer. We are happy to discuss what structure works for your situation.

data.question: Are your attorneys licensed and in good standing?

children.text: Yes. All attorneys at Caldwell & Associates are licensed members of the State Bar in good standing. Our firm carries professional liability (malpractice) insurance and adheres to the Rules of Professional Conduct. You can verify attorney licensure through the State Bar's public directory.

data.question: How do I schedule a consultation?

children.text: You can call us at (555) 234-5678, use the contact form on our website, or email us directly. Our office is staffed Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM to 5:30 PM. We will respond within one business day to confirm your appointment.

data.question: Is what I tell you confidential?

children.text: Yes. Attorney-client privilege protects communications between you and our attorneys from disclosure to third parties. This applies from the moment of your initial consultation. We cannot be compelled to reveal what you tell us in confidence, and we take that obligation seriously.
